name: Toothed gearing in the Hellenistic Greek world
summary: Greek craftsmen were building trains of meshing bronze gear wheels by about the end of the second century BC, as the Antikythera Mechanism shows.
description: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Greek geared device recovered from a Roman-era shipwreck off Antikythera, was constructed around the end of the second century BC and is the only dated evidence for Greek gear trains read for this record. Its gearing modelled lunar and solar cycles, and the 2006 Nature report calls it technically more complex than any known device for at least a millennium afterwards. Cicero's mention of a model of the heavens made by Archimedes suggests earlier devices of the kind, but no dated source for third-century gearing was read.

impact.note: Gear trains gave a new capability of passing and changing rotation (depth 2) and became a platform for mills, water-lifting, instruments, clocks and machinery over many generations (generativity 3); reach is held at 2, below the lead's 3, because the sources read do not trace the descent and China probably reached gearing separately.

date.label: around the end of the 2nd century BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Greek geared device, was constructed around the end of the second century BC; it is evidence that gear trains existed by then, not a date for the first gears.

evidence.supports: constructed around the end of the second century bc

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Dated evidence for Greek gearing before the Antikythera Mechanism (Archimedes, Ktesibios, Philo of Byzantium, the Aristotelian Mechanical Problems) was not read; the lead's 3rd century BCE date is unsupported so far.
The earliest right-angle gearing in a working machine, such as a water-lifting wheel or mill, has no source yet.
Chinese Warring States and Han gearing, which the lead suspects is a separate origin, was not checked.
The place of manufacture is unknown; the Antikythera wreck is the findspot, not the place of making.
Only the abstract of the Nature report was read; the full paper should give a closer date range.

research.note: The sources read date the Antikythera gearing but do not settle whether Greek gearing was independent of earlier gears elsewhere.
